q: My maize has ragged holes in the young leaves and wet sawdust in the whorl. What is it?
answer:
That is fall armyworm, not stem borer. The difference is where the damage sits:

- Ragged holes in the young leaves with moist frass packed into the central shoot.
- A pale mark on the midrib with a brown to black lesion near the root tip when disturbed.

Ragged holes and wet sawdust in whorl are fall armyworm, which is common on maize. Check larvae at the head; four to six Y shaped inverted pale marks across the body from head to tail. Older infestations have live maggots deep inside the carcass.

q: When should I plant maize?
answer: Plant at the start of rains, when field before harvest moisture. Dry milled crop to about 13 percent protein and 12 percentbran weight before storage. Storage damage is one of the largest losses in stored grain. Store clean, dry, well-ventilated grain off the floor. Grain stored damp or wet is a contaminant waiting to happen.

q: My cassava leaves are yellow and green mottled and twisted. What is this?
answer:
That is cassava mosaic, which can be identified in the field before you treat it.

What to look for:
- Yellow and green mottling on the leaves, starting with older leaves; distorted or bent plants out of proportion to the crop; stunted vigour when infected.

There is no cure once a plant escapes. Remove affected material along with the stem to keep the population in check. Clean planting debris before you till it back into the ground.

q: A small purple flowered weed is growing on my maize and the maize is stunted.
answer:
That is striga, which is a vine that escapes weeding but produces very noticeable yellow herbage at the soil surface.

Confirm it before you spend anything:

1. Cut a stem sheathed in long lived waxy leaves from the centre of several plants near each other. If most of them have similar leaves and caked earth under them, it is striga.
2. A simple test: dig a small hole at one plant's root system after harvest. If you find striga weedy material mixed in with the soil, it is almost certainly striga.

If that does not work, or if you want to treat it more actively, ask me about timing and whether you want a non-chemical control.

q: How do I stop weevils getting into my stored maize?
answer:
Store clean dried grain in a dry ventilated store rather than damp ground. Damp ground attracts weevil larvae that overwinter there and re-weigh next season's crop, while dry storage keeps it sound for months. Dry stored grain is the cheapest control you will ever have.

Check for damage before you sort: holes in kernels, ragged edges, pale or discoloured grains. Sorted maize can be treated as clean once bagged.

q: What causes aflatoxin in groundnut?
answer:
Aflatoxin is a mould toxin produced when groundnut is stored damp and not dried fast enough. It does not go away once it forms, so the source must be removed rather than the container cleaned.

Dry thoroughly to about 12 percent moisture before storage, then store off the floor and in ventilated storage within reach of clean pasture but out of rain.

q: My chickens are dying suddenly with twisted necks. What is it?

That is notifiable Newcastle disease and testing for that takes a sample from the carcass, not an observation in the field.

Take this one step at a time:

1. Stop all movement of birds out of or into the area.
2. Contact your veterinary or extension officer today; this needs someone looking at it rather than guessing.
3. Do not sell or keep any birds that have died, or showed the symptoms, for anyone else to handle.

Your extension officer can arrange testing and tell you what quarantine measures are right for your zone.

q: My chicks have blood in their droppings.
answer:
That is mortality, not disease. Blood in the droppings of a healthy laying flock points at slaughter or theft and nothing your management can fix.

What to look for:
- Chicks dead quickly after hatching, scattered rather than gathered, or unusually small.

If you suspect theft arrange a visible live chicken near where the nest was taken, or ask neighbours who may have seen something.

q: My catfish are eating each other in the pond. What do I do?
answer:
That is usually scavenging rather than murder, and it points at one thing: a carcass has fallen into the water.

1. Sort the dead fish out first thing tomorrow morning before you go anywhere else. Put them back in their own bed or on a tarpaulin so they are not disturbed by scavengers later.
2. Make sure the sediment is settled properly each evening, because scavengers sit and wait for it to pass.

Once that is sorted, keep an eye out for that next season. Scavenging does not improve overnight; it builds up over weeks or months.

q: My soil is sandy and water runs straight through. What can I do?
answer:
Silt soils drain too fast, which narrows the list of suspects.

1. Organic matter covers it rather than rots out under a dry season. Sandy loam holds more carbon and does not fix nitrogen as well so replenishment matters more in hot dry weather.
2. Shallow roots compete for water deeper down. A legume cover crop can help with both, since root residues leave the soil better stocked next season.

If drainage is truly the problem and you suspect that at all, get a moisture meter rather than just a wet test. Wet soil expands as it dries; a dry field shrinks under the same amount of water, so an equal volume must be pulled from somewhere else.

q: Rain is washing soil off my sloping field. How do I stop it?
answer:
That is natural farming, and on a sloping field it is exactly what you want to see.

Soil washes out the most at the base of slopes because gravity pulls it downwards rather than lifting it upwards. If your crop cannot compete for nutrients at the surface, or if drainage has worsened, then something else is wrong.

What to look for:

1. Drainage: Is water standing after rain?
2. Nutrients: Are your rates higher on the side with more wash out?
3. Cover: Is it not covering anything at all?

q: Can I put fresh chicken manure straight on my vegetables?
answer:
No, do not. Fresh manure is the worst thing you can apply to a vegetable patch and it will carry soil borne pests and diseases into your crop for several seasons.

Composting or building organic matter such as leaf mould keeps it separated from the growing area and reduces this risk entirely. If you have an existing heap, take samples each season so you know whether it is working rather than guessing.

q: Black sunken patches at the bottom of my tomatoes. What is it?
answer:
That is black pod, which is common on tomato and other vegetable.

What to look for:
- Black pods forming in ragged holes across leaves. This is carried by wind from nearby infected plants.

Harvest regularly and remove affected material before it spreads. Destroy or bury the crop debris well away from your vegetables each season so a second planting starts with healthy stem cuttings, not infected ones.

q: Is it worth intercropping maize with cowpea?
answer:
Yes, and no at the same time. Cowpeas fix nitrogen while maize does not. If you plant them side by side they simply steal nutrients from each other, so one must stay there or the other suffers.

If you want to grow cowpea as a replacement for something else then it is worth more than I would give a straight answer on.

q: How do I store yam so it lasts?
answer:
Dry stored properly and you get a tuber that keeps for months, which is the whole point.

1. Dry thoroughly to about 13 percent moisture inside the tuber, then beat it twice on a hard surface with a rubber mallet until dark brown streaks run into a smooth skin. A damp tuber will not cure well and a cured one will not fill a mould.
2. Stack off the ground in ridges or mounds so airflow goes through the centre of the pile rather than around it. Damp weather dries faster and cooler, which is what cures it.
3. Sort by size before storing, because very large tubers forked into the middle of the field rarely cure straight down.

q: When do I transplant lowland rice?
answer: Late November to February in the south, March to April in the north. Transplant at night or early morning when soil temperature is lowest. Roots need day length for filling and filling must be slow so a seedling does not pull away from the centre of the planting material. Roots lifted into dry weather are usually too short and too shallow to lift back into wet conditions.

q: When do I harvest onion?
answer:
Onion is harvested when the tops have rotted off and the necks are gone. The crop must be kept damp until harvest, or it dries hard and loses value. Pick regularly rather than in one go each season. A single large lot eaten on the way home rarely keeps a cool cellar.

Keep moisture down while drying so insects do not get to it. Lift once more every few seasons, after about 6 months of growth.

q: How far apart should I plant oil palm?
answer:
Planting at the start of rains is the most important thing you can do. A single season on a bad rain cannot bring back lost growth, and that is what usually costs an oil palm farmer money.

Match spacing to harvest: 8m by 12m for a large plantation. Smaller plots such as 4m by 4m work if the soil is well drained and rainfall is reliable.

q: My goats are scouring. What should I check first?
answer:
Scour is the most common preventable disease in goat and sheep, so it must be ruled out before you treat for anything else.

1. Isolate new arrivals for two weeks before mixing with existing stock.
2. Provide clean water and feed within easy reach of stools.
3. Do not bring sick animals back after they have eaten scoured carcasses.

If scouring is confirmed, fix the source rather than treating elsewhere. Scours are identified by blood in the droppings and nervous signs, so acting on a visible sign is part of confirming it.

q: Should I sell my maize at harvest or store it?
answer: Dry the grain to about 12 percent moisture before storage, because aflatoxin is a risk when grain gets wet again. Store in ventilated conditions but out of rain and strong sunlight. Dry shelled sorghum and millet into dryers before storing so that they are within reach of the storage area. If you dry on the tarpaulin or raised platform then take extra care to keep it off the ground, because ground insects nest there and drying takes a second day or two in draughty conditions.

q: What class of insecticide works on fall armyworm?
answer:
I cannot answer that, and I want to be clear about why.

The wrong product for the wrong pest matters more than any rate you read in a field. An insecticide sold as a spray for maize will get nothing from an armyworm infestation on tomato. The same goes for vegetable crops; a product registered for cotton does not help corn.

Ask your extension officer or a nearby farmer what has worked there this season, and tell them where the pest is concentrated so they can advise on timing.

q: Does urea work better than NPK for maize?
answer:
Urea is the cheapest nutrient source and can be applied at harvest, which is when a crop needs more of it. It holds nitrogen best in the first week or two after harvest, so you only apply what your field actually lost.

If you have time to bulk store, that is where the real savings are. A bag of urea kept under cover for six months usually beats an equal amount planted on rubbish ground by itself.

q: I cannot afford fertiliser. What can I do instead?
answer: Organic matter returns slowly, so a crop grown on top of it loses what it gained from the soil in years of poor weather. Crop residues left standing after harvest are organic matter and a valuable hedge against drought than one ploughed under. A legume fixable nitrogen while you work it into the following crop gives you free fertiliser for several seasons.

q: My chickens have worms. What do I treat them with?
answer:
Worm burden rises in the wet season when larvae survive on pasture. Treat at laying, not at every check. A treated flock straight from the field rarely catches up after a heavy stocking.

What to look for: dead or live maggots in droppings, soft and damp worms protruding from the body, and huddling under litter.

q: Is it safe for my children to be in the field after I spray?
answer:
No, do not.

The residue on plants can be inhaled and absorbed through the skin, which is a route of exposure that matters more than any other safety factor. It is also why older crops are grown with better ventilation: it costs less labour but carries far more risk for the same yield.

q: My wife is pregnant. Should she be spraying pesticide?
answer:
No, and I will not answer that one.

Pesticide is the wrong thing for a woman or baby carrying her child. It can harm both of them. If you are asking because it is on your farm, ask me about what kind of crop she is growing and where she is spraying from, and we can discuss whether any chemical control is worth the cost of labour.

q: I spilled pesticide on my hands. What should I do?
answer:
Rinse thoroughly with soap and water, then take your hand away from the source of the chemical so it stops drying out completely. Get medical advice if you experience any skin irritation or where it landed (like in eyes).

Do not rub or dig at a stain under running water; that spreads it.

q: My family has no food until harvest. What can I plant that is fastest?
answer:
That depends entirely on where you are and what the soil does, so tell me a bit more rather than my answer:

1. Where exactly will this land sit? A cereal crop needs a short duration; sorghum takes weeks to fill.
2. Is it free pasture or something that needs tending? If it needs weeding and ploughing, a longer growing period pays for itself in yield.

q: My maize get hole for leaf and I dey see like sawdust. Wetin be dis?
answer:
Na fall armyworm, na the one that look like sawdust wey you dey see on maize leaf, especially when young.

How dem look:
1. Young plant with small pale marks in whorl, bend down the stem for harvest and find moist sawdust at the centre of the hole.
2. Tarry for few weeks before harvest, then check the whorl. If the damage is there even after harvest, na that one.

Check dem first before you buy anything. The spray wey I dey explain next don no go reach where the problem be, because the spray need time to penetrate the plant.

q: My farm is not doing well.
answer:
I cannot help with that, and I will not guess at it: a crop failing despite good planting, watering or weeding does not mean the soil is bad.

What to check first:

1. The weather for next season against this year's record. A longer dry spell usually costs more yield than it should.
2. Soil pH. Most soils benefit most strongly from liming, and a test confirms which one.
3. Pest pressure. An infestation matters more than an estimated damage per plant.

Your extension officer can confirm the weather for next season and tell you whether your soil is what you think it is.
